title: Anns Decision

jokes.text: I'm gonna get 12 eggs and part of a dead animal. Dealer's choice. Please and thank you.
jokes.setup: A casual diner ordering scene is established — Ann orders oatmeal and berries.
jokes.punchline: 'Part of a dead animal. Dealer's choice.' — Leslie's cheerful, maximally carnivorous order delivered with bureaucratic politeness.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly efficient cold-open joke. 'Dealer's choice' applied to meat is absurdly specific and perfectly Leslie — cheerful, maximalist, unbothered by social norms. 'Please and thank you' on top seals the character voice. High economy: three phrases do a lot of heavy lifting to establish Leslie's personality for any new viewer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'll have the egg white omelet, but I need you to use free-range, organic, cage-free eggs from hens that have been played classical music and given names. I want the peppers diced to exactly one-quarter inch—no smaller, no larger. The toast should be from a multigrain loaf that was stone-ground using a 19th-century French millstone. And could you please make sure the hash browns are arranged in a fibonacci spiral? Also, I have some questions about your supply chain.

jokes.text: Ann orders catfish and grits with pumpernickel toast as her 'new thing' while dating herself.
jokes.setup: Ann explains she's 'dating herself' and ordering one typical thing plus one she'd never order.
jokes.punchline: The 'adventurous' order is catfish and grits — mildly unconventional food, not the thrilling reinvention her framing implies.
jokes.explanation: Mild observational comedy about Ann's concept of 'dating herself.' The gap between the self-discovery framing and the mundane execution (catfish and grits) is the joke, but it's subtle and doesn't land hard. Functions more as exposition setup than a real joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm going to stop trying to find a guy and just focus on myself. I'm going to be my own best friend.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm going to be my own two best friends. And we're all beautiful.

jokes.text: Now I have two best friends, Ann and Ann. Each one more beautiful than the other.
jokes.setup: Ann explains her self-dating experiment — she has two sides of herself, represented by different food choices.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately adopts the concept and flatters both imaginary Anns, treating them as real separate best friends.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie-Ann relationship humor. Leslie's extravagant flattery of Ann is a running character trait, but applying it to two hypothetical Anns is a fresh twist. 'Each one more beautiful than the other' is logically impossible and utterly sincere — peak Leslie. High quotability and strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So Ann, how was the skydiving?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh, it was amazing! I was so brave up there, I didn't even think about how I could die.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's great!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, until we landed and I immediately threw up and cried for twenty minutes.

jokes.text: Which Ann is screaming like a maniac? Oatmeal Ann or catfish Ann? I'm not sure, because I instantly blacked out from extreme terror.
jokes.setup: Ann shows her skydiving blog photo. Leslie asks which 'Ann' (oatmeal or catfish) is screaming.
jokes.punchline: Ann admits she blacked out from terror, undermining the adventurous self-dating narrative entirely.
jokes.explanation: A solid two-beat joke: Leslie's absurd question about which Ann is screaming (which extends the earlier bit beautifully), followed by Ann's self-deprecating confession of blacking out from terror. The callback to the earlier Ann duality and the deflation of Ann's adventurous arc make this land well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, we should totally go ice skating together! It'll be so fun!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm taking myself on a date.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Perfect! So it's a double date. You and you, me and Ben. This is going to be amazing!

jokes.text: Yeah, we'll do a double date: You and you, and me and Ben.
jokes.setup: Leslie suggests Ann take herself ice-skating as a blog idea.
jokes.punchline: Leslie frames it as a 'double date' — two Anns plus Leslie and Ben — treating the two-Ann concept as a genuine social arrangement.
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Leslie treating the two Anns as real people continues with a logical extension — proposing a double date. It's consistent and characterful, though diminishing returns compared to the initial two-Ann joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you are smart, you are funny, you are kind, you are talented, you are generous, and you are stupid hot. I mean, that's just a fact.

jokes.text: But I have to warn you, I'm very good at ice-skating. I can do jumps. You know what? I probably shouldn't come. I'll embarrass the both of you.
jokes.setup: Leslie suggests the ice-skating double date.
jokes.punchline: She earnestly warns that she's so good at ice-skating she'll embarrass everyone and maybe shouldn't come — completely sincere self-assessment.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie overconfidence delivered completely straight. The joke is in the sincerity — she genuinely believes she's so athletically superior she'd embarrass her friend. The escalation from 'I can do jumps' to 'I probably shouldn't come' is well-structured. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you can't just decide to have a baby in six weeks. That's not how this works.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Why not? Women do it all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, they don't. Unless you're Channing Tatum's wife, in which case, congratulations, but that's the only acceptable scenario.

jokes.text: Ann, you know that I fully support any woman's decision — especially a beautiful unicorn-nurse like yourself — in creating the family that she wants. But you are so brilliant and kind and stupid hot.
jokes.setup: Ann reveals she wants to go to a sperm bank today to become a single mother.
jokes.punchline: 'Stupid hot' as a compliment, buried inside what is ostensibly a supportive speech but is actually Leslie pivoting immediately to flattery and subtle discouragement.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's Ann-worship reaching peak levels: 'beautiful unicorn-nurse' and 'stupid hot' are genuinely funny coinages. The comedy comes from the structure — Leslie opens with a feminist declaration of support and immediately undermines it with pure flattery. 'Stupid hot' is highly quotable and feels authentically Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I think there's been a mistake. I ordered the rib eye steak. This appears to be a bowl of chopped up leaves and twigs. Is this what you feed the horses?

jokes.text: Ann is giving up on love and deciding to have a baby with herself. And she has only been dating herself for six weeks. If she were dating a guy for six weeks, and they decided to have a kid, I'd be like, 'Congratulations, Ann... And Channing Tatum.' Because that is the only scenario that would make sense to me.
jokes.setup: Leslie's talking head about Ann's decision to use a sperm bank after six weeks of 'dating herself.'
jokes.punchline: The only man Leslie could imagine Ann appropriately having a six-week baby with is Channing Tatum — her benchmark for perfection.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The logic is airtight: Leslie sets up a normal concern (six weeks is too fast to have a kid) then reveals that even in the hypothetical, she'd only approve if it were Channing Tatum. The 'Congratulations, Ann... And Channing Tatum' pause is perfectly timed. It works on character (Leslie's Ann idolization, her impossible standards), on structure (slow build to specific celebrity punchline), and is supremely quotable. Compares favorably to the 8.0 anchor example.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why would you only serve salad at your wedding if you were a rabbit?

jokes.text: What a gorgeous herbaceous medley. There's been a mistake. You've accidentally given me the food that my food eats.
jokes.setup: A catering tasting for the wedding. Ron is served a salad.
jokes.punchline: 'You've accidentally given me the food that my food eats' — Ron's complete disdain for vegetables framed as a polite correction to a logistical error.
jokes.explanation: The best joke of the episode and one of the best Ron Swanson lines in the series. 'The food that my food eats' is a genuinely brilliant construction — logically coherent (animals eat plants), perfectly economical (eight words), and could only come from Ron. The phrase 'gorgeous herbaceous medley' as sarcastic acknowledgment before the pivot is the setup working at full efficiency. This is calibrated above the 8.0 anchor and approaches the 9.5 anchor in craft and impact. Cultural touchstone-level line for Parks and Rec fans.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom is an expert on food. He knows everything about farm-to-table, locally sourced ingredients, artisanal preparation techniques.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, I just know that if food is expensive and comes on a tiny plate, people think it's good.

jokes.text: Salad is traditionally the first course at a wedding. Is a gerbil marrying a rabbit?
jokes.setup: Someone defends the salad by noting it's traditional for a wedding first course.
jokes.punchline: Ron asks if the wedding guests are small herbivores, implying only animals would eat this food.
jokes.explanation: An immediate callback and escalation from joke #9. Ron extends the 'salad is animal food' premise into a logical question about the guest species. 'Is a gerbil marrying a rabbit?' is a perfectly absurd image delivered with Ron's characteristic deadpan. Extremely quotable, strong character integration, excellent economy. Nearly matches the previous joke's quality — these two form a legendary one-two punch.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is a perfectly adequate crudités. The vegetables are arranged in a way that suggests someone put thought into it, but not so much thought that it becomes interesting. The dip—which I'm assuming is some sort of ranch situation—has that familiar tang of disappointment.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know, this pasta has a certain je ne sais quoi. Which is French for 'I don't know what,' which is also how I feel about this pasta.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The chicken is exquisite. It tastes like chicken that knows it's chicken but wishes it was something better. Like a duck.

jokes.text: Tom's food review: 'Number two's was subtle and provocative, like a coy Dutch woman guarding a dark secret. Number three's told a story — a story from a book I wouldn't read but I would watch the movie of.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks Tom which caterer he liked. Tom is supposed to give a useful opinion.
jokes.punchline: Tom delivers impenetrable pseudo-intellectual food criticism that provides zero useful information — culminating in 'a book I wouldn't read but I would watch the movie of.'
jokes.explanation: Peak Tom Haverford absurdist food criticism. 'A coy Dutch woman guarding a dark secret' is a wild non-sequitur that somehow feels like something Tom would genuinely say. The escalation to 'a book I wouldn't read but I would watch the movie of' is the standout line — perfectly constructed, specific, quotable, and character-perfect. The 'Nothing you're saying is helpful' response from Ben validates what the audience is thinking.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The umami profile is quite sophisticated. It's a delicate balance of—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? I have no idea what I'm talking about. I don't read.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But this gazpacho is cold, and that's all I need to know.

jokes.text: Number three's told a story -- a story from a book I wouldn't read but I would watch the movie of.
jokes.setup: Tom continues his food review in an increasingly pretentious, useless way.
jokes.punchline: The food told a story from 'a book I wouldn't read but I would watch the movie of' — perfectly captures Tom's pseudo-intellectual laziness.
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff of Tom's pretentious food critic bit and it's genuinely excellent. 'A book I wouldn't read but I would watch the movie of' is a killer line — it perfectly characterizes Tom as someone who performs cultural literacy without effort, and the structure (I wouldn't X but I would Y) is crisp and quotable. Justifiably one of the episode's standout lines.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's a delicate hand-crafted artisanal pocket of dough, filled with a curated selection of premium ingredients, each one sourced from the finest purveyors in the tri-state area, folded with precision and baked to a golden perfection that represents the pinnacle of appetizer engineering.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's a calzone.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yes, but—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A small calzone.

jokes.text: Ben insists on calling the mini-calzone a 'savory pastry' — 'a delicate little dough pocket filled with tomato sauce, cheese, and seasoned meat. Just a stunning culinary innovation.' 'It was a calzone. It was literally just a small calzone.'
jokes.setup: Ben loved the mini-calzone appetizer and describes it in elaborate, pretentious terms.
jokes.punchline: The hard flat statement: 'It was a calzone. It was literally just a small calzone.' — destroying Ben's foodie pretension.
jokes.explanation: This sets up a running gag that pays off spectacularly later. Ben's elaborate redescription of a calzone is funny on its own (the gap between his reverence and the mundane reality), but the flat, repeated 'It was literally just a small calzone' is the structure doing its best work. Excellent comedic economy in the deflation. The calzone becomes a recurring element and the betrayal callback is some of the episode's best material.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're not a couple. We're best friends. Although I understand the confusion given our obvious chemistry and the way we finish each other's sentences and occasionally touch each other's hair.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But no, we're not lesbians. Although if we were, I'm sure we'd be very good at it.

jokes.text: No. Tragically, we are both heterosexual.
jokes.setup: The sperm bank receptionist asks if Leslie and Ann are a couple.
jokes.punchline: 'Tragically, we are both heterosexual' — implying Leslie wishes they could be together.
jokes.explanation: Three-word punchline that perfectly encapsulates Leslie's devotion to Ann. 'Tragically' is doing enormous comedic work — it's deadpan, character-perfect, economical, and deeply quotable. The joke works because it's 100% in character for Leslie to genuinely lament not being able to be Ann's partner. One of the episode's most quotable lines.

dialogue.speaker: Worker
dialogue.line: What are you looking for in a donor?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, someone with good genes, obviously. Tall, athletic, good teeth, no genetic diseases.

dialogue.speaker: Worker
dialogue.line: Right, and what about personality traits?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh! Well, I guess someone who's generous? Like, willing to give of themselves?

jokes.text: What are you looking for in particular? 'Some sperm.' I meant in terms of a donor? 'Oh, you know, nice guy... Nice sperm.'
jokes.setup: The receptionist asks what Ann is looking for, meaning donor characteristics.
jokes.punchline: Ann takes it literally ('some sperm'), then when clarified, gives the delightfully vague answer 'nice guy... nice sperm.'
jokes.explanation: A clean two-beat joke. The first beat (literal misunderstanding) is standard, but the second beat is where it earns its score — 'nice guy... nice sperm' is perfectly vague and endearingly simple, as if Ann has thought deeply about this and arrived at the most obvious possible criteria. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my God, a Harvard-educated donor is coming to visit the Parks Department!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, that's great, but let's be realistic. He's probably going to take one look at our budget, our facilities, and our general incompetence, and then donate all his money to literally any other organization in the country.

jokes.text: Oh, you know, nice guy... Nice sperm.
jokes.setup: Receptionist asks what Ann is looking for in a donor.
jokes.punchline: Ann's criteria: 'nice guy... nice sperm' — winningly simple and slightly absurd.
jokes.explanation: The capper to the previous beat. 'Nice sperm' as a requirement is innocently funny — it's the logical extension of 'nice guy' and simultaneously meaningless as actual criteria. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Cycling is great exercise. It's low-impact and really builds leg strength.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I love cycling. Lance Armstrong is a hero.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, Lance Armstrong cheated. He used performance-enhancing drugs.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, but he looked really cool doing it.

jokes.text: This guy went to Harvard! 'So did the Unabomber.'
jokes.setup: Ann and Leslie flip through the sperm donor binder. Ann is excited about a Harvard-educated donor.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately cites the Unabomber as a Harvard alumni to shut down the suggestion.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie-sabotage joke — she's dismissing every candidate. The Unabomber pivot is a well-known comedy device (prestigious institution + infamous alumnus), but it's deployed efficiently here and Leslie's ulterior motive (steering Ann away from ALL donors) adds a layer of character comedy. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Joe here is a convicted felon.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: I sure am.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's true, I looked it up.

jokes.text: This guy seems healthy. Loves cycling. 'Yeah, so did Lance Armstrong, and he turned out to be a lying drug user. Or a hero. I don't know where we stand on him now.'
jokes.setup: Ann finds a healthy, cycling-enthusiast donor.
jokes.punchline: Leslie invokes Lance Armstrong, then undermines even THAT takedown with genuine uncertainty about his cultural status.
jokes.explanation: The Lance Armstrong joke benefits from perfect timing — this episode aired right when the Armstrong scandal was fresh, making the 'I don't know where we stand on him now' line a funny acknowledgment of real cultural confusion. The self-undermining of Leslie's own sabotage attempt is the structural highlight. Still very effective years later as pure character comedy.

jokes.text: Sewage Joe appearing at the sperm bank — the man who was fired for emailing a picture of his penis to every woman in city hall.
jokes.setup: Ann and Leslie are at the sperm bank reviewing donors. Someone they know walks in.
jokes.punchline: It's Sewage Joe — introduced by Leslie with his full criminal history — and he's a donor here.
jokes.explanation: Great recurring character deployed for maximum cringe comedy. The casual, matter-of-fact way Leslie introduces Joe's history ('the gentleman who was fired for emailing a picture of his penis to every woman in city hall') is perfect — Leslie always frames things in the most bureaucratically polite way possible. Joe's 'Guilty' followed by 'Yeah, that's what the judge said' is a clean two-beat callback to his own crimes.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that outfit looks great on you.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, you look really nice today.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You look like a beautiful, magical horse. No wait—a unicorn. Actually, scratch that—a sexy, sexy mermaid.

jokes.text: 'Guilty.' 'Yeah, that's what the judge said.'
jokes.setup: Joe casually admits to the penis-emailing crime by saying 'Guilty' as a greeting.
jokes.punchline: Leslie dryly points out that 'guilty' is what the judge literally found him — recontextualizing his casual admission as an actual legal verdict.
jokes.explanation: A compact gem. Joe says 'Guilty' meaning something like 'yep, that's me,' and Leslie immediately deadpans that yes, that's what the judge determined. The double meaning of 'guilty' — casual admission vs. legal verdict — is exploited with perfect economy. One of the cleanest joke structures in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I feel like I could tell someone their parents just died in a mall fire, and they'd just nod and thank me for the information.

jokes.text: Joe: 'Free money, free porn. Best job I ever had. Also... if you're looking to buy some weed, I'm looking as well.'
jokes.setup: Joe confirms he's a sperm donor and explains the appeal.
jokes.punchline: He pivots from describing the donor perks to soliciting a drug connection — the 'also' implying this is a natural continuation of the conversation.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation — the 'Also' transition makes the weed solicitation feel like it's on the same natural list as 'free money, free porn.' Joe is a wonderfully functional cringe character and this moment efficiently delivers a third beat of wrongness.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm going to be sick. Is this a Banana Republic? I can't even look at this place. It's like if a khaki had a baby with a polo shirt and they raised it in a country club.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This store is giving me hives. I need to leave before I do something I regret, like set this place on fire or organize their clearance section by color.

jokes.text: Leslie has tried on eight different outfits for Ben. 'Babe, you look super hot.' 'You realize you've said that about all of them?' 'Well, she has, every single time. 'Cause she is super hot.'
jokes.setup: April watches Ben evaluate Leslie's eighth outfit attempt. She notes he's said the same thing each time.
jokes.punchline: Ben doubles down with complete sincerity — he genuinely means it every time, and April's exasperation validates how ridiculous this is.
jokes.explanation: Warm character comedy about Ben's hopeless devotion to Leslie. April as the weary observer makes it funnier — her exasperation contrasting with Ben's earnest sincerity. Not a groundbreaking joke but well-executed and characterful.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What is all this stuff in your pockets?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, well, let's see. I have a photo of me and Ben at the Sweetums factory tour, a receipt from the first waffle I ever bought in Pawnee, ticket stubs from when we saw Neutral Milk Hotel at the Civic Center, and a handwritten note that Jerry wrote me that says 'You're doing great.'

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's somehow worse than if you had just murdered someone.

jokes.text: Honestly, you'd look hot naked.
jokes.setup: Ben has said all outfits look super hot; April challenges this.
jokes.punchline: Ben's ultimate defense: even no clothes would be the best option, delivered as a sincere logical conclusion.
jokes.explanation: A good payoff beat to the outfit sequence. Ben's sincere devolution to 'you'd look hot naked' as a logical endpoint is funny because he means it earnestly, not lewdly. Economy is strong — it's four words that do exactly what they need to.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm wearing all black because I'm very serious.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's cool. You know what we should do? We should start a band called Fleetwood Mac.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Fleetwood Mac already exists.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Ugh. This suit makes me want to scold a Catholic child.
jokes.setup: April is trying on Leslie's pantsuit to impersonate her for a public forum.
jokes.punchline: The suit's stern authority-figure aesthetic makes April want to perform the most specific, darkly funny act of institutional authority she can imagine.
jokes.explanation: An outstanding line. 'Scold a Catholic child' is a perfect April Ludgate construction — darkly specific, not gratuitously offensive, and perfectly characterizes both the suit's energy AND April's personality. The unexpected specificity of 'Catholic child' elevates it above a generic 'this suit makes me look strict' joke. High originality, excellent economy, and could only come from April. One of the episode's top-tier jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, why don't we just call the band Fleetwood Mac?

jokes.text: I don't know who Ann Taylor is, but I hate her and I want to kill her.
jokes.setup: April is wearing a conservative Ann Taylor pantsuit, unhappy about it.
jokes.punchline: She mistakes the clothing brand 'Ann Taylor' for a real person and threatens her — a perfect April misunderstanding delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A deceptively clever joke. April's literalism — treating a clothing brand as a real enemy — is completely in character. 'I hate her and I want to kill her' delivered as a calm conclusion is pure April. The joke works through misdirection (we expect a fashion complaint, we get a death threat) and the brand-as-person misunderstanding. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, I wouldn't use Eagleton sperm if I were you. Have you seen the men there? It's like someone took all the extra chromosomes and made a town.

jokes.text: The discovery that Leslie's pants have a sewn-in Fleetwood Mac concert ticket stub from 1995 in a secret pocket.
jokes.setup: April examines Leslie's pantsuit more closely, wondering what's in the pocket.
jokes.punchline: A Fleetwood Mac concert ticket from 1995 — confirming that Leslie has had this suit for decades and considers this pocket treasure.
jokes.explanation: A great visual detail joke about Leslie's character. The 1995 Fleetwood Mac ticket tells you everything about Leslie Knope — the suit is ancient, she keeps mementos of joyful experiences everywhere, and she's never thrown anything away. The specificity of 1995 is perfect. This is character comedy through prop work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Our ideal donor is someone who's generous, philanthropic, community-minded, and hates jazz.

jokes.text: Fleetwood Mac Sex Pants. New band name. I call it. 'Ooh, you know what? Maybe just Fleetwood Mac.'
jokes.setup: April dubs the pants 'Fleetwood Mac sex pants' after learning their history.
jokes.punchline: Andy excitedly claims it as a band name, and April drily suggests maybe they should just call the band 'Fleetwood Mac' — pointing out that already exists.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Andy/April two-hander. Andy's earnest band-name enthusiasm followed by April's deadpan suggestion that the name already exists is a clean, well-timed joke. It's funny because April is subtly pointing out that Fleetwood Mac Sex Pants is a worse name than the band that already has a similar name — but she says it as though she's being helpful. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I believe in women's autonomy, self-determination, and the right to make our own choices without male interference.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann is my best friend and I respect her independence completely. By the way, Ann, you're wearing that outfit tomorrow whether you like it or not.

jokes.text: Fleetwood Mac Sex Pants. New band name. I call it. Ooh, you know what? Maybe just Fleetwood Mac.
jokes.setup: April coins the phrase 'Fleetwood Mac Sex Pants.'
jokes.punchline: Andy claims it as a band name, then immediately suggests just calling it 'Fleetwood Mac' — unaware Fleetwood Mac already exists.
jokes.explanation: Andy's 'maybe just Fleetwood Mac' — delivered with genuine enthusiasm as if he's had an original idea — is a perfect character joke. It requires Andy to not know Fleetwood Mac exists, which is completely plausible for him, and the beat of thinking he's improved on April's joke by stripping it to its essence is perfectly constructed. High character integration — only Andy Dwyer would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, Dave from HR may not be the sharpest tool in the shed, and yes, he did sexually harass me that one time, but the man has heart. And I think it's wrong that we're eliminating him just because he's incompetent and creepy.

jokes.text: Leslie sabotaging the sperm donor search by talking about how Ann needs to know his 'favorite season of Friends, whether or not he hates jazz — hopefully, he does.'
jokes.setup: Leslie argues Ann should ideally know the donor personally.
jokes.punchline: Her list of essential personality traits includes 'favorite season of Friends' and 'hates jazz — hopefully he does' — revealing Leslie's very specific dealbreakers.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy. The idea of 'favorite season of Friends' as a vetting criterion is funny on its own, but 'whether or not he hates jazz — hopefully he does' is the kicker: Leslie is projecting her own preferences onto Ann's ideal partner. It subtly reveals that Leslie's support is conditional on the baby daddy sharing Leslie's values.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Harris
dialogue.line: Well, I appreciate the recognition, but I should mention that I've actually been doing this work longer than most people in this office have been alive.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Harris
dialogue.line: My research has been cited more times than probably anyone else in this building. Not that I'm counting.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Harris
dialogue.line: But I am counting.

jokes.text: Leslie's confessional: 'In this case, the body is Ann's, and the woman in charge of it is me.'
jokes.setup: Leslie declares she fully believes a woman should be in charge of what happens to her own body.
jokes.punchline: She immediately applies the principle to mean SHE (Leslie) is the woman in charge of Ann's body.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's structural comedic peaks. The setup is Leslie performing feminist rhetoric, and the punchline completely inverts the principle by making Leslie the authority over Ann's body. It's satirical, character-perfect, and the logical structure is airtight. The irony is layered: Leslie isn't malicious, she genuinely believes this is FOR Ann. Extremely quotable and a defining Leslie Knope moment.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Harris
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, the good news is he can't run away from me.

jokes.text: Leslie eliminated 'Knuckle-hair Dave from HR.' 'I don't mind the knuckle hair. I just think he's a dick.'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains how she narrowed down the candidate list by eliminating 'obvious no's' including Knuckle-hair Dave.
jokes.punchline: Ben's reason for excluding Dave is not the knuckle hair (which he'd tolerate) but his personality — a weirdly specific and admirably fair character judgment.
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan beat. The specificity of 'Knuckle-hair Dave' as a character we never meet is funny, and Ben's clarification that the knuckle hair is FINE but Dave's personality is the real problem is a nice subversion of the obvious joke. Economy is high.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I think I have food poisoning. I'm probably going to die. How am I supposed to date if I'm dead?

jokes.text: Dr. Harris: 'The seats in my office are leather.' followed by 'Small office. Mine's way bigger.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is running a fake job interview to screen sperm donors, and Dr. Harris is unaware he's being evaluated.
jokes.punchline: Harris keeps casually establishing his superiority through material possessions — leather seats, bigger office — as small talk, completely unaware this is a vetting session.
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy establishing Dr. Harris as an arrogant, materialistic guy — which explains why he's quickly eliminated as a candidate. The jokes are mild but serve the plot and character efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I've been sick for three days straight. I've lost seven pounds.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Seven pounds? That's like... me and a half.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's exactly right.

jokes.text: Chris's food poisoning confessional: 'I'm dying. I was dying earlier today. And then I died. Now I'm dead.'
jokes.setup: Chris, who always claims to be the healthiest person alive, appears in a talking head.
jokes.punchline: He delivers a tragic soliloquy about dying in which he escalates past 'dying' to declaring himself already dead — each beat more dramatic than the last.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant subversion of Chris's defining character trait. Chris is famously health-obsessed and optimistic about his physical perfection — having him react to food poisoning with escalating declarations of death ('I was dying... then I died... now I'm dead') is perfect. The dramatic escalation of tense (present to past to present-tense death) is a precise comedic structure. One of the episode's standout character moments.

jokes.text: Chris: 'I had to cancel a date with Shauna Malwae-Tweep. And I really like her. Do you think she'll still like me now that I'm dead?'
jokes.setup: Chris is devastated by food poisoning and declares himself dead.
jokes.punchline: His concern shifts to whether Shauna will still date him now that he is (in his mind) dead — treating his hyperbole as literal.
jokes.explanation: A lovely extension of joke #32. Chris commits fully to the death metaphor and extends it into relationship anxiety — the absurdity of 'will she still like me now that I'm dead?' is funny because Chris treats it as a genuine logistical problem. Strong character integration with Chris's romantic sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm going to try this Leslie thing. I'm going to be enthusiastic and inspiring.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're going to change this town. We're going to make a real difference. Together, we can—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Is that a dead rat?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: There's a dead rat right there. On the ground. By your foot.

jokes.text: Ben: 'I did not sleep for one second last night. And I cracked the bottom of the toilet bowl.'
jokes.setup: Multiple characters are suffering from food poisoning. Ben describes his night.
jokes.punchline: 'I cracked the bottom of the toilet bowl' — an extreme physical consequence implying the violence of his digestive illness, delivered as a matter-of-fact complaint.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly calibrated gross-out joke that earns its impact through understatement. 'I cracked the bottom of the toilet bowl' is extreme enough to be shocking but delivered so flatly it reads as genuine complaint rather than boast. The image is vivid without being graphically described.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Wait, this interview is about me? I thought you were just here to document my daily routine because I'm so fascinating.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: How often does this happen? Because I'm assuming it's at least once a week.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I have voided more than Tom's body weight in the last 12 hours alone.'
jokes.setup: The group worries about Tom, wondering how he must be feeling given his small size.
jokes.punchline: Ron quantifies his own output in relation to Tom's total body mass — a precise, dignified, deeply wrong statement delivered with Ron's characteristic gravity.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional Ron joke. The comedy comes from Ron's dignity in quantifying something deeply undignified — measuring his illness in units of Tom's body weight is both absurd and oddly logical for Ron's empirical personality. It's also a great size joke about Tom without making Tom the butt of the joke directly. Extremely quotable and competes with the salad jokes as a top Ron moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. That was impressive. I respect the hustle.

jokes.text: April's public forum opening: 'As Eleanor Roosevelt once said to Betty Ford: "Hillary Clinton is great."'
jokes.setup: April is attempting to impersonate Leslie at a public forum, opening with a quote as Leslie would.
jokes.punchline: The 'quote' is fabricated — Eleanor Roosevelt and Betty Ford never met to discuss Hillary Clinton — and the content is completely generic, revealing April's total failure to do any research.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly layered joke. On the surface: a fake quote. The comedy comes from multiple angles: (1) the historical impossibility (Roosevelt died before Clinton was known), (2) the generic content of the 'quote' (it says nothing), (3) April's failure to understand WHAT makes a Leslie quote work, and (4) April's complete confidence in delivering it. Deeply April, deeply funny. High marks across craft dimensions.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Yo, it's me, The Douche. I'm like a low pressure system moving in from the west, baby. You can feel me coming, and when I arrive, everything's gonna be wet.

jokes.text: April distributes 'friendship bands' she made and announces the audience members are now 'Park Pals.'
jokes.setup: April announces there's a 'special surprise' under the chairs — audience members expect something official.
jokes.punchline: Handmade friendship bands and the declaration that they're now 'Park Pals' — April's DIY, slightly threatening version of Leslie's warmth.
jokes.explanation: A good cringe-comedy beat. April attempting Leslie's warm community-building approach but producing something subtly strange (unsolicited friendship bands from a government employee) is funny. The audience's presumed discomfort is part of the joke. 'Park Pals' as an April-invented term has a forced corporate-friendly ring that's inherently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I feel like I've been poisoned by a bad clam. My insides are staging a coup d'état against my outsides.

jokes.text: 'You should see the booger under this chair.'
jokes.setup: Audience members are looking under their chairs for friendship bands.
jokes.punchline: Andy, apparently seated in the audience, reports finding a booger instead — a wonderfully childish observation.
jokes.explanation: A short, effective Andy joke. The booger observation is perfectly in character — Andy is genuinely curious and child-minded, so of course he notices and reports this. The timing (interrupting April's sincere attempt at a Leslie moment) makes it funnier. Simple but earns its score through character authenticity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have a very strict rule about sauce. I never eat sauce that's been applied by someone else's hand. It has to be on the side, and I apply it myself in a very specific ratio.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Also, I only eat at restaurants where they know my name, where I've established a relationship with the chef, and where they comp my meal at least once every three visits.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'That son of a bitch is astute.'
jokes.setup: Pete immediately identified that Ann wanted his sperm, blowing Leslie's cover completely.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, in a confessional, reluctantly acknowledges Pete's perceptiveness using a mild profanity that sounds extremely funny in Leslie's typically wholesome register.
jokes.explanation: A five-word joke that's nearly perfect. The comedy comes from the collision of Leslie's polished, government-professional speech register with 'son of a bitch,' and the fact that the insult is immediately paired with a genuine compliment ('astute'). It's surprised, reluctant respect expressed through mild profanity. Extremely quotable. One of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Calzones. It was calzones all along.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: From this moment forward, I declare war on calzones. Eternal war. I will hunt them down wherever they exist. I will not rest until every calzone in this city has been destroyed or removed from existence.

jokes.text: Pete: 'When will women in this town stop scheming to get my sperm?'
jokes.setup: Pete has identified the scheme and confronts Ann and Leslie.
jokes.punchline: He frames this as a recurring experience — apparently women regularly scheme to acquire his sperm, which is both absurd and a funny implied compliment to himself.
jokes.explanation: The follow-up to Pete's revelation. Framing this as a RECURRING problem for him in Pawnee adds an absurd layer of self-aggrandizement. 'Women in this town' implies this is a Pawnee-specific epidemic. Good escalation from the previous joke.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: I'm concerned about the safety of this park.

dialogue.speaker: Walter
dialogue.line: Safety? I'm afraid of birds. All birds. Even the small ones.

dialogue.speaker: Walter
dialogue.line: And escalators. What if my pant leg gets caught?

dialogue.speaker: Walter
dialogue.line: Also, I'm terrified of the letter Q. It's just an O with a tail. Who decided that was okay?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This is the worst safety briefing I've ever heard.

jokes.text: Howard Tuttleman's entrance: 'I know it's a winter's morn, but it feels like a summer's eve, 'cause "the douche" is in the building.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann await their final candidate. Leslie needs to identify who 'Howard Tuttleman' is.
jokes.punchline: He introduces himself as 'The Douche' with a seasonal metaphor — 'summer's eve' being both a season and a feminine hygiene product, making the douche reference literal on two levels.
jokes.explanation: A clever entrance. 'Summer's Eve' is a feminine hygiene brand (douche), making The Douche's entrance line function as wordplay on two levels simultaneously — seasons and hygiene products. The setup ('winter's morn') gives the pun room to breathe. Well-crafted for what is essentially a character introduction.

jokes.text: Tom walks into the food-poisoning sick room: 'Whoa! Smells like some vomit took a dump in here.'
jokes.setup: Tom arrives to find his colleagues suffering from food poisoning.
jokes.punchline: His description of the smell — 'vomit took a dump' — is a vivid, hierarchical grossness escalation: the secondary product of an already gross thing.
jokes.explanation: A good gross-out simile with some craft behind it. 'Vomit took a dump' is a two-level escalation (the smell is worse than vomit — it's what vomit would excrete). Tom's obliviousness to how poorly timed his observation is makes it funnier. He's describing his colleagues' suffering as an aesthetic failing.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen 1
dialogue.line: We should build a statue of Harris!

dialogue.speaker: Citizen 2
dialogue.line: Yeah! A statue of Harris!

dialogue.speaker: Multiple Citizens
dialogue.line: Harris! Harris! Harris!

jokes.text: Tom reveals he didn't get food poisoning because of 'Haver-food rule number six — never eat anything with a sauce I have to dip myself. Drizzle it on for me. I'm not your maid.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is confused about how Tom avoided the food poisoning — he ate the same food.
jokes.punchline: He didn't eat the mini-calzones because of an elaborate personal food rule about self-dipping — a rule so specific and dramatic it only makes sense as Tom Haverford logic.
jokes.explanation: A superb payoff to the calzone setup from earlier. Tom's immunity to the food poisoning is explained by a food rule so specific and diva-ish it's absurd — 'I'm not your maid' about dipping one's own food is a peak Tom Haverford statement. 'Haver-food rule number six' implying there are at least six such rules is great worldbuilding. The character integration here is exceptional — this joke could genuinely only come from Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You could do a whole show about how women are terrible drivers and terrible at math.

dialogue.speaker: Howard
dialogue.line: That's... that's actually not a bad idea.

jokes.text: Ben: 'The calzones... betrayed me?' 'Never again, guys. As God as my witness, they're dead to me.'
jokes.setup: Ben learns the calzones caused the food poisoning.
jokes.punchline: Ben's response treats the calzones as sentient traitors worthy of a Scarlett O'Hara-level dramatic declaration — 'As God as my witness, they're dead to me.'
jokes.explanation: The emotional payoff of the entire calzone arc. 'The calzones... betrayed me?' is a perfect beat — Ben anthropomorphizing the food he defended passionately earlier in the episode. The pivot to a Gone with the Wind-level oath ('As God as my witness, they're dead to me') about mini-calzones is both absurd and deeply in character for Ben, who takes everything (food included) very seriously. One of the most quotable lines of the episode and a genuine rewatch moment. Compares favorably to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: All right, well, Tommy feels great. And I'm about to go eat some lasagna. Peace!
jokes.setup: Ben has just dramatically renounced calzones; the entire team is sick.
jokes.punchline: Tom cheerfully announces his lasagna plans and exits with 'Peace!' — completely indifferent to his colleagues' suffering.
jokes.explanation: Tom's breezy exit while his colleagues suffer is a clean character joke. The 'Peace!' sign-off while announcing lasagna plans is perfect Tom Haverford — self-absorbed and oblivious in the most charming way.

dialogue.speaker: Howard
dialogue.line: We could name them something meaningful, like after a family member or a beloved historical figure. Or we could go with something fun and creative, like Streetlamp or Bouillabaisse or Captain Thunderpants McGillicuddy.

jokes.text: Tom: 'All right, well, Tommy feels great. And I'm about to go eat some lasagna. Peace!'
jokes.setup: Everyone is devastated by food poisoning; Tom is the only healthy one.
jokes.punchline: Tom announces he's about to eat lasagna (pasta with sauce) and exits cheerfully — completely unmoved by his colleagues' suffering.
jokes.explanation: A clean tag to the food poisoning arc. Tom's cheerful announcement of lasagna plans to his suffering colleagues is perfectly callous, and 'Peace!' as an exit is very Tom. The lasagna choice is a small grace note — it's also a baked dish with sauce, but apparently differently classified by Haver-food rules.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I am the captain of a sinking ship, and Ann is the rat that abandoned me. No wait, that's not right. Ann is the ship, and I'm the rat. No, actually, I'm Moses, and Ann is the Red Sea, and I'm trying to part her, but she's closing in on me, and I'm going to drown. Except the Egyptians are also drowning, so we're all drowning together.

jokes.text: The topless park escalation: 'I'm afraid this park will raise my taxes.' / 'I'm also afraid the park will be noisy. And full of spiders. And dark at nighttime. I'm scared of a lot of stuff. Everything's fine. I'm fine. I'm Walter, and I'm fine.' / 'Is this gonna be a topless park?'
jokes.setup: April is running a public forum about the Pawnee Commons park project. Audience members voice concerns.
jokes.punchline: The concerns escalate from legitimate (taxes) to anxious (spiders, dark at nighttime) to self-aware ('I'm scared of a lot of stuff') to non-sequitur ('Is this gonna be a topless park?').
jokes.explanation: A great public-forum escalation sequence. 'I'm scared of a lot of stuff. Everything's fine. I'm Walter, and I'm fine.' is a wonderful moment of anxious self-awareness from a background citizen — the self-reassurance while admitting broad fear is genuinely funny. The pivot to 'topless park' is the absurdist punchline that caps the sequence perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Howard
dialogue.line: We're taking calls about Ann Perkins' romantic situation. Caller, you're on the air.

dialogue.speaker: Howard
dialogue.line: That's right, folks. Ann's been getting absolutely railed lately. Her love life is a complete dumpster fire.

dialogue.speaker: Howard
dialogue.line: She's gone through more men in this town than I've had sandwiches for lunch, and believe me, that's a lot of sandwiches.

jokes.text: Woman: 'If this is going to be a topless park, I won't sign your petition.' / Other man: 'If she's going to the topless park, I'm not signing the topless park petition.' / 'You know, I take that back, I'm still in.'
jokes.setup: The topless park idea has been raised and is now dividing the community.
jokes.punchline: A man initially opposes the topless park due to social pressure but immediately recants — 'I take that back, I'm still in' — revealing his true position.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation on the topless park joke. The structure of the man caving to social pressure then immediately reversing is a quick, efficient laugh. 'I'm still in' is a nicely casual admission of his real feelings.

jokes.text: After the topless park idea spreads, Harris from the food poisoning storyline appears: 'Yeah, yeah. Forget whatever that Pawnee Commons is. I'm with that pervert. Topless park. Topless park!'
jokes.setup: The topless park chant breaks out at the forum.
jokes.punchline: Harris (a recurring name from the sick-room scenes) appears to join the topless park chant — a cross-storyline cameo that escalates the mob mentality joke.
jokes.explanation: Functional escalation beat. The spread of 'topless park' from one eccentric citizen to a chanting mob is good mob-mentality comedy. Harris's involvement adds a familiar face to the chaos.

jokes.text: The Douche's backstory: Northwestern semiotics major, wrote a thesis on 'narrative forms in the digital world' — then became a morning shock-jock and invented 'taint ball.'
jokes.setup: Ann asks The Douche where he went to school, expecting to find him shallow.
jokes.punchline: He's a Northwestern semiotics major with a serious academic thesis who voluntarily chose to create 'taint ball' and do fart jokes — the gap between his potential and his profession is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly rich character comedy beat. The reveal that The Douche is a serious academic who deliberately chose his shock-jock persona as satire that 'snowballed' is genuinely interesting and funny. The contrast between 'semiotics thesis on narrative forms in the digital world' and 'invented taint ball' is a maximal gap joke. It humanizes the character while keeping him ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What happened with the forum results?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, we had a pretty good turnout. There was this one guy, Rodney Dangerfield, who asked a really insightful question about the zoning ordinances.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Well, I think you probably need to get back to the studio, play some fart jokes, make fun of some immigrants.' The Douche: 'Actually, a farting immigrant segment would be really funny.' 'Ay dios...'
jokes.setup: Leslie sarcastically describes The Douche's radio content to dismiss him.
jokes.punchline: The Douche immediately takes her sarcasm as a pitch and genuinely likes the segment idea — and then produces a sample Spanish phrase, committing to the bit.
jokes.explanation: Good irony reversal — Leslie's dismissive sarcasm becomes an accidental pitch meeting. The Douche's 'Ay dios...' self-audition is a funny commitment to a bad bit, and it happens so fast the audience barely has time to process it. The structure works because Leslie causes the very thing she's criticizing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: JJ, this food is amazing. You really outdid yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Seriously, best meal we've had all year.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, JJ, you're a culinary genius.

dialogue.speaker: JJ
dialogue.line: Thanks, guys. I really appreciate that.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, didn't we all get food poisoning last time JJ cooked for us?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, we spent six hours at the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I lost twelve pounds in one day.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: And yet here we are, praising him like he just won a James Beard Award.

jokes.text: 'Good looking out, Leslie. You guys ever want to do this again, sans clothing, give me a shout.' 'That was the douche talking.'
jokes.setup: The Douche wraps up the conversation and makes a final comment about nudity.
jokes.punchline: 'That was the douche talking' — Howard's way of distancing his genuine self from his persona's inappropriate comments, used as a recurring tag.
jokes.explanation: 'That was the douche talking' functions as a running gag throughout The Douche's scenes — a persona disclaimer that never quite does the distancing work Howard intends. The joke is that 'the douche' and Howard are clearly one and the same, and the disclaimer fools no one. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: And we're back with Leslie Knope from the Parks Department. Leslie, we've been talking about your job, and I gotta say, I have an idea for a product that could really help you. It's called Fartsicle.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, what?

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Fartsicle. It's a popsicle that you insert into your rectum, and then you fart it out into someone's face.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... that's not a real product.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Not yet. But think about it. You got your fruity flavors, your grape, your cherry, your butterscotch. You're welcome, America.

jokes.text: 'I'm gonna scan a quick pic of them boobies for a little deposit in "El banco de spanko."' / 'That was the douche talking.' / 'Douche nation.'
jokes.setup: Howard wraps up the meeting with a final inappropriate comment about the women.
jokes.punchline: Howard deploys the 'El banco de spanko' coinage, disclaims it as the douche, then immediately adds 'Douche nation' — tripling down in the disclaimer itself.
jokes.explanation: The 'that was the douche talking' disclaimer running gag pays off most when Howard immediately undercuts his own apology with 'Douche nation' — proving the disclaimer is meaningless. 'El banco de spanko' is a funny coinage even if the surrounding content is crude.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: This is The Douche with your traffic and weather update. There's a baby on the road! I'm calling this situation 'Operation: Baby on Board.'

jokes.text: Howard asks Ann and Leslie where the library is immediately after exiting.
jokes.setup: Howard has just delivered an elaborate exit full of bravado.
jokes.punchline: He immediately breaks character to ask where the library is — suggesting he's lost in the building and deflating the dramatic exit.
jokes.explanation: A clean punctuation joke on The Douche's exit sequence. The abrupt deflation from his exaggerated persona to a mundane navigational question is a classic comedy technique — and the library specifically (a place of quiet, intellectual pursuit) is the right environment for the incongruity. Well-timed and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Howard Tuttleman
dialogue.line: We'll make the deal, but only if you agree to one condition.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Okay, what is it?

dialogue.speaker: Howard Tuttleman
dialogue.line: You have to dress up like Clair Huxtable from The Cosby Show, but only the episodes from seasons 3 through 5, and you can't wear any outfit she wore more than once in the series.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's... very specific.

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: We don't make the rules!

jokes.text: Howard: 'If we had a little girl, I would name her Elizabeth, after my grandmother. She was this strong, amazing woman. And if we had a boy, I don't know, I'd name him something funny, like "Dick" or "O.J."'
jokes.setup: Leslie has revealed Ann's plan to Howard. He responds thoughtfully about having children.
jokes.punchline: Howard pivots from a heartfelt tribute to his grandmother into suggesting naming a son 'Dick' or 'O.J.' — both comic (Dick) and darkly loaded (O.J.) names.
jokes.explanation: A great character-consistent joke. The structure is classic misdirection: establish that Howard has depth (loving tribute to grandmother) then immediately undercut it with comedy. 'Dick or O.J.' is a two-beat punchline where the first is crude wordplay and the second is dark cultural reference — both bad baby names for very different reasons. It confirms Howard is Howard AND the douche simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fine, I'll do it. What do you want me to impersonate?

dialogue.speaker: Howard
dialogue.line: I want you to impersonate me accurately.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... that's the whole thing. That's what impersonating someone means.

dialogue.speaker: Howard
dialogue.line: Exactly. And I want it to be accurate.

jokes.text: Leslie's devastated confessional: 'My God. I have driven Ann right into the belly of the douche.'
jokes.setup: Leslie realizes her plan to stop Howard from being chosen has backfired — she revealed everything to Howard, who is now enthusiastic about the plan.
jokes.punchline: 'Into the belly of the douche' — a twist on 'belly of the beast' that is horrified, dramatic, and accidentally crude.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Into the belly of the douche' is a perfect phrase — it riffs on 'belly of the beast,' applies it to Howard's radio persona ('The Douche'), and in doing so creates an unintentionally anatomical image that Leslie is completely oblivious to. It's funny as wordplay, funny as Leslie's horrified self-realization, and funny as an image. Extremely quotable and a standout confessional moment. Compares favorably to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, this isn't my bag. Where is my Leslie Knope costume?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, I grabbed the wrong one. That's my gym bag.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your gym bag? Andy, I need the wig, the blazer, the whole thing. We're supposed to be there in twenty minutes!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Just wear what's in there. Be creative.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: There's a half-eaten protein bar, a sweatband, and... is this a Pokemon card collection?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Holographic Charizard. Mint condition. You're welcome.

jokes.text: Howard broadcasts Ann's sperm search on his radio show: 'Remember that chick Ann I used to... Yeah, she was smoking hot! Turns out, she wants to have my baby... And it's down to me and some other turd-munchers.'
jokes.setup: Leslie told Howard everything, trusting him to be reasonable. We hear what he did with the information.
jokes.punchline: He immediately broadcast it on his radio show — referring to other candidates as 'turd-munchers' — completely violating the confidentiality.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe payoff. The reveal that Leslie's trust was immediately violated is not surprising but it's well-executed. 'Turd-munchers' is a classically juvenile Douche-persona insult that lands because it's so specific and pointless. The segment title 'Operation Baby Douche' seen in the next scene extends the cringe appropriately.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: The parks department budget is allocated based on several factors including maintenance costs, staffing, and community programs.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: So what does that cost?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It varies by year and department needs.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: Yeah, but how much is it? I want the exact number, but I don't want you to use any numbers.

jokes.text: Anyway, her lesbo friend tells me she's on the prowl for some baby beans... And it's down to me and some other turd-munchers.
jokes.setup: Howard continues his on-air segment about Ann's donor search.
jokes.punchline: 'Baby beans' for sperm and 'turd-munchers' for the other candidates are Howard's characteristically crass radio vocabulary.
jokes.explanation: 'Baby beans' is a funny euphemism, and 'turd-munchers' for the competing donors is peak shock-jock vocabulary. Somewhat lowbrow but character-appropriate for Howard.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Don't call me ma'am. I work for the government.

jokes.text: Um, crappy. We only got four signatures. Two of them were me and Andy, and one of them said 'Farts McCool.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks how the public forum went.
jokes.punchline: The forum netted four signatures: two from organizers, one fake name ('Farts McCool'), and one unaccounted for — a disaster report delivered flatly.
jokes.explanation: 'Farts McCool' is a perfectly chosen fake name — specific, dumb, and funny. The breakdown of the four signatures (two organizers, one fake) is a classic Parks and Rec civic failure joke delivered with perfect April deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No. We're not having a topless park. Not now, not ever. If I see one breast in that park that isn't a bird, I will personally hunt you down and make you regret every decision that led to this moment.

jokes.text: Well, I'm feeling so much better. Almost no weird stuff snuck out of my body last night.
jokes.setup: Chris is recovering from food poisoning.
jokes.punchline: 'Almost no weird stuff snuck out of my body last night' — a deeply euphemistic way to describe recovery from violent food poisoning, delivered with Chris's typical cheerful positivity.
jokes.explanation: 'Almost no weird stuff snuck out of my body last night' is a brilliant Chris Traeger line — he describes catastrophic bodily expulsion in the most delicate, positive-spin possible terms. 'Almost no' and 'snuck out' do all the work. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Harris, you're incompetent, useless, and nobody likes you.

dialogue.speaker: Harris
dialogue.line: Yes! More! Tell me how much I disappoint you!

jokes.text: This might sound crazy, but Jean-Ralphio has started a catering company. He has? Now, granted, he is currently standing trial for counterfeiting Euros, but the trial's gonna be over quick. He's definitely guilty. Ugh, forget it.
jokes.setup: The group needs a new caterer for the wedding.
jokes.punchline: Tom pitches Jean-Ralphio's catering company — the caveat being he's on trial for counterfeiting Euros, and Tom immediately concedes 'he's definitely guilty.' Ben just says 'Ugh, forget it.'
jokes.explanation: A great Jean-Ralphio joke delivered without Jean-Ralphio. The escalation of 'he's currently on trial for counterfeiting Euros' as a mere caveat, followed by Tom's own pre-emptive conviction of his friend ('he's definitely guilty'), is pitch-perfect. 'Ugh, forget it' from Ben is the clean button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, I'm sorry. You're right, I can be controlling sometimes. From now on, I'm going to trust you to make your own decisions.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But I've color-coded a binder for you with tabs and dividers organized by decision category, a laminated reference guide for optimal choices, and a spreadsheet tracking your progress. I've also created a flowchart you can follow.

jokes.text: The Douche's radio show: 'We, uh, got an update on "Operation... Baby douche." / Leslie walks in and the Douche plays a 'me so horny' sound effect. Leslie: 'That was not me. That was a farcical sound effect.' / 'Did she say fartsicle? The fartsicle. Frozen farts you can eat. Put it in your face-mouth!'
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives at the radio station to confront The Douche. He immediately incorporates her into his show.
jokes.punchline: The sequence escalates from embarrassing sound effect → Leslie's flustered correction → 'fartsicle' mishearing → full product development of 'fartsicle: frozen farts you can eat.'
jokes.explanation: A good escalating cringe sequence. The mishearing of 'farcical' as 'fartsicle' is the comedic engine, and 'Frozen farts you can eat. Put it in your face-mouth!' is absurdist product description humor at a decent level. The whole sequence reflects Leslie being completely out of her depth in shock-jock territory.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, what is all this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, these are my planning materials for the new community center. I've been working on slogans. How about 'It's a Cute-rus!' Get it? Cute? Uterus? Because it's a space for women's health and wellness!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've got seventeen more!

jokes.text: Okay, we're back. We, uh, got an update on 'Operation... Baby douche.'
jokes.setup: Howard returns to his radio show to update listeners on Ann's situation.
jokes.punchline: 'Operation Baby Douche' as the formal name of the segment covering Ann's reproductive plans.
jokes.explanation: 'Operation Baby Douche' as a formalized mission name is funny — it's the kind of segment name a morning shock-jock would actually use. The operatic naming of something this private is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, why do you have a folder labeled 'Baby Names' next to your computer?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, that's just my womb with a view collection. I've been organizing my uterus for success.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Your... what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, I watch a lot of cartoons. I've picked out 47 potential baby names, and I've color-coded them by cuteness level. Also, I may have already decorated a nursery in my mind using only things from the Pottery Barn kids catalog.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, you don't even have a boyfriend.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not yet. But when I do, he's going to be so impressed by my organizational binders.

jokes.text: 'Me so horny.' That was not me. That was a farcical sound effect. Did she say 'fartsicle'? The fartsicle. Frozen farts you can eat. Put it in your face-mouth! It's cold and it smells. God, how did you make that so fast?
jokes.setup: Leslie appears on Howard's radio show to defend Ann's privacy; Howard immediately plays an inappropriate sound effect.
jokes.punchline: The 'fartsicle' product — 'frozen farts you can eat' — invented and hawked in seconds by Howard and Ira, escalating from sound effect to full product pitch.
jokes.explanation: The 'fartsicle' gag escalates quickly and is committed to with gusto — 'put it in your face-mouth, it's cold and it smells' is a funny product description. Leslie's exasperated 'God, how did you make that so fast?' is the perfect straight-man response. This is lowbrow but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's amazing! You're going to be such a great mother!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, actually, I haven't decided if I want to adopt or use a surrogate or—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm just so proud of you!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, you just said I'm going to be a great mother. Don't you want to know how I'm planning to do this?

jokes.text: The Douche: 'I will lay off if you can survive one round with Breasty Bertha in... The Jell-O Pit!'
jokes.setup: Leslie demands The Douche stop talking about Ann on air. He negotiates a deal.
jokes.punchline: The negotiating leverage is surviving one round with 'Breasty Bertha' in a Jell-O pit — the completely disproportionate terms offered by a shock-jock.
jokes.explanation: Standard shock-jock absurdity but executed well. 'Breasty Bertha' as a name is exactly right for this character. The logic of the negotiation (silence = Jell-O wrestling) is absurd in the way The Douche consistently is.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, you were amazing out there. You really nailed it. I'm gonna go home tonight and think about you in that outfit... for like, six hours.

jokes.text: Leslie negotiates the Jell-O wrestling terms: she'll stand there for ONE SECOND and say 'Rudy.' The reason: 'Cause The Cosby Show.' / 'Classic.'
jokes.setup: Leslie agrees to minimal Jell-O pit participation — just standing there and saying one word.
jokes.punchline: The word is 'Rudy' — referencing The Cosby Show — and The Douche's 'Classic.' response treats this as legitimate nostalgia.
jokes.explanation: A funny negotiation beat. The absurdity of the terms — Leslie will say 'Rudy' once, for The Cosby Show — and The Douche treating this as a meaningful cultural tribute ('Classic') makes for a good odd-couple moment. Leslie maintaining her dignity through the most undignified possible bargain is characterful.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you burned my suit?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You left it on the chair. I didn't know it was there.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So it's my fault?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, if you didn't want your suit burned, maybe don't leave it where suits get burned.

jokes.text: I am a city councilwoman, so I am not gonna Jell-o wrestle. I mean, this is fun. Don't you want your constituents to know that you got a fun side?
jokes.setup: Leslie refuses to Jell-o wrestle; Howard uses civic rhetoric to tempt her.
jokes.punchline: Howard appeals to Leslie's desire to connect with constituents — a perfect political argument for Jell-o wrestling.
jokes.explanation: Howard's use of constituent-relations language to justify Jell-o wrestling is a nice ironic twist. Leslie's constitutional weakness to civic duty makes this a character-specific joke — Howard has found her exact pressure point.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, why are you burning my suit?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You said I could do whatever I wanted today.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I didn't mean burn my clothes!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You should've been more specific.

jokes.text: Rudy. [pause] No, say it like Bill Cosby. Rudy. / I don't know. / Yeah! / Oh, she's touching her boobs now. / No, I'm not. I'm just standing here.
jokes.setup: Leslie is standing in the Jell-o pit saying 'Rudy' — trying to do a Bill Cosby impression she clearly can't do.
jokes.punchline: Howard's accusation that Leslie is 'touching her boobs' in the Jell-o; Leslie's mortified denial.
jokes.explanation: The Jell-o pit sequence is cringe comedy — Leslie Knope forced into a shock-jock degradation ritual while maintaining total dignity. The 'touching her boobs' accusation + 'No, I'm just standing here' is a good cringe beat.

jokes.text: Leslie in the Jell-O, quoting The Cosby Show: 'Theo, now there's Jell-O all over my favorite sweater.' Then The Douche announces: 'And the gold medal goes to Leslie Knope!'
jokes.setup: Leslie has fallen into the Jell-O and is now covered in it.
jokes.punchline: Leslie can't help making a Cosby Show joke even while humiliated — quoting Theo/Cliff dialogue about a sweater — and The Douche pivots to declaring her the winner.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's instinct to quote The Cosby Show even while covered in Jell-O is peak character comedy — she can't help making a relevant cultural reference even in humiliation. The Douche declaring her the 'gold medal' winner despite her obvious loss is a funny reframe that turns her defeat into something Leslie can live with.

jokes.text: April discovers she has the wrong bag — full of Fruit Roll-Ups and baseball cards instead of Leslie's pantsuit.
jokes.setup: April needs to change into the Leslie pantsuit for the next forum. She asks Andy for the bag.
jokes.punchline: The bag contains Fruit Roll-Ups and baseball cards — a perfect inventory of what Andy would pack instead of a professional outfit.
jokes.explanation: A great Andy-specific joke. The contents of his bag — Fruit Roll-Ups and baseball cards — are exactly what a man-child would prioritize over professional attire. It's character comedy through prop work, and the specificity of the two items tells you everything about Andy. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Look, you look amazing in this outfit. Plus you're the smartest person on the planet. I think you can do this just being yourself.'
jokes.setup: April is panicking because she doesn't have her Leslie costume and props for the forum.
jokes.punchline: Andy's sincere, loving encouragement — April is already competent and doesn't need to be Leslie — is funny because of his complete obliviousness to having caused the problem.
jokes.explanation: Warm character moment. Andy's sincere belief in April is sweet and funny — he's clearly not grasping the professional stakes. Not a high-craft joke but performs important emotional work in the episode and is characteristically Andy.

jokes.text: I don't have my Leslie pantsuit or my Leslie headband or my Leslie notes. I can't do this meeting without my Leslie stuff.
jokes.setup: April realizes she has none of Leslie's props for the next forum.
jokes.punchline: 'My Leslie stuff' as a formal category of equipment needed to impersonate Leslie Knope.
jokes.explanation: April's itemization of 'Leslie stuff' as a kit she needs is charming — it implies she's been assembling an impersonation toolkit. A lighter character moment but consistent and warm.

jokes.text: Citizen: 'Yeah, I didn't ask for a math lesson. So why don't you just tell me how much it's gonna cost me? And don't use numbers.'
jokes.setup: April gives a percentage breakdown of the project funding. A citizen interrupts, annoyed.
jokes.punchline: 'Don't use numbers' as a demand — the citizen objects to mathematical communication itself.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully efficient joke about public ignorance and bureaucratic frustration. 'Don't use numbers' is a genuinely funny demand because it's the most logical extension of 'don't make this complicated' — taken to an absurd extreme. The citizen isn't hostile, just genuinely averse to numerical communication. Highly quotable and a great Pawnee-citizen character beat.

jokes.text: April's response to the citizen: 'Look, you won't have to pay any extra money, okay? And don't ever call me "ma'am" again. Thanks. Next question.'
jokes.setup: A citizen demands no numbers and called April 'ma'am.'
jokes.punchline: April answers the money question simply, then pivots to a personal grievance about being called 'ma'am' — as though that's the pressing issue — and just moves on.
jokes.explanation: April being April — handling the legitimate question efficiently while firmly asserting a personal grievance about honorifics. 'And don't ever call me ma'am again. Thanks. Next question.' is perfect April cadence: the 'thanks' makes it somehow more menacing. High character integration and great economy.

jokes.text: Harris (the stoner from the forum) is back: 'Yeah, I wanted to talk more about that topless park idea that a local hero brought up yesterday.' April: 'There's not gonna be a topless park, Harris. Nobody wants your creepy stoner eyes staring at them while they're enjoying a park, okay? Stop being gross.'
jokes.setup: April is running the second forum as herself. Harris returns with the topless park agenda.
jokes.punchline: April's response is unfiltered and specific: 'creepy stoner eyes' is a precise diagnosis that's more personal than a formal refusal — and it works.
jokes.explanation: April's confrontational style emerges fully when she's being herself rather than Leslie. 'Creepy stoner eyes' is a vivid, specific insult that's funny precisely because it's accurate rather than diplomatic. It's also the 'being herself' arc paying off — April is MORE effective as herself.

jokes.text: Harris: 'Shut me down! You scare me, and I gotta say, I kinda dig that.'
jokes.setup: April firmly shuts Harris down about the topless park.
jokes.punchline: Harris's arousal at being intimidated — 'I kinda dig that' — is a perfectly absurd character reaction that turns the rejection into an inadvertent compliment.
jokes.explanation: A funny character beat. Harris's masochistic appreciation of April's dismissal subverts the expected dynamic (intimidation shuts him down) and extends his characterization as someone who operates on entirely different social frequencies. 'Shut me down!' is a great reaction exclamation.

jokes.text: Andy: 'What's your deal?' / Harris points to April. Andy: 'She's married to me.'
jokes.setup: Harris expresses interest in April after she intimidates him.
jokes.punchline: Andy's flat 'She's married to me' — delivered presumably with zero aggression, just as information — is a perfect Andy moment: completely without territorial posturing.
jokes.explanation: Four words that do exactly what they need to. Andy isn't threatened, isn't boastful — he just states the fact. The comedy comes from how un-macho it is and how perfectly it suits Andy's good-natured obliviousness. The economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: April's confessional about the radio station: 'But they did invite me to participate in their topless Jell-O-lympics... So that's something.'
jokes.setup: April reports back on how the radio station experience went.
jokes.punchline: 'So that's something' — April's deadpan acknowledgment that being invited to 'topless Jell-O-lympics' is a mixed outcome, delivered as though weighing pros and cons.
jokes.explanation: A great April deadpan. 'Topless Jell-O-lympics' is a wonderful compound noun, and 'So that's something' is April being sincerely uncertain whether this is good or bad. The understated delivery of a completely absurd achievement works perfectly in confessional format.

jokes.text: Councilman Milton appears out of nowhere: 'Councilman Milton, do we have a meeting?' / 'Oh, no, no, no. I just wanted to toss my name into the ring, in respect to this Indian woman's vagina.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is dealing with the Ann situation. Councilman Milton — an older, oblivious council member — appears.
jokes.punchline: He's nominating himself as a sperm donor, referring to Ann as 'this Indian woman' (Ann is not Indian) and using the word 'vagina' in the council hallway.
jokes.explanation: A sharp cringe-comedy beat. Milton's obliviousness combines ethnic misidentification (Ann is not Indian) with clinical terminology deployed in completely inappropriate contexts. The joke is about the kind of older male entitlement that inserts itself everywhere. 'In respect to this Indian woman's vagina' is an unhinged formulation that earns the laugh.

jokes.text: Is that a drawing of my reproductive system saying 'Let's do this'? The Knope way involves a lot of uterine cartoons. What can I tell you?
jokes.setup: Leslie presents Ann with her color-coded binder for the sperm donor process.
jokes.punchline: The binder contains a drawing of Ann's uterus saying 'Let's do this' — the visual gag of Leslie having drawn Ann's reproductive system with a motivational caption.
jokes.explanation: Leslie having drawn Ann's uterus with 'Let's do this' written on it is a perfect Leslie Knope joke: obsessively supportive, visually expressive, slightly bizarre. 'The Knope way involves a lot of uterine cartoons' as a matter-of-fact explanation is Leslie at her most self-defining. High character integration.

jokes.text: Leslie's drawing of Ann's reproductive system labeled 'Let's do this.' / 'What is more cuter-us than your uterus?'
jokes.setup: Leslie presents Ann with a color-coded binder to help with the sperm donor decision, including uterine cartoons.
